Onshore, offshore, upstream, FID: the oil and gas words explained

By the Katelago HR team

Namibia has an oil and gas sector now, and with it has come a vocabulary that most of us were never taught. Business owners sit in meetings where people talk about blocks, FIDs and FPSOs and nod along, which is a poor basis for deciding whether to bid for something.

This is a plain explanation of the words, written for managers and business owners rather than engineers. Where a term has a specific meaning in Namibian law, we say so. Where it is simply industry usage, we say that too.

Onshore and offshore

Onshore means on land. In Namibia, that is mainly the Kavango basin in the north east, where exploration and testing have been under way for several years.

Offshore means at sea. Namibia's significant discoveries are offshore, in the Orange Basin off the south west coast, in water depths reaching around three thousand metres. Anything below roughly five hundred metres of water is usually called deepwater, and Namibia's discoveries sit well into that category.

The distinction matters more than it sounds for anyone thinking about work in the sector. Offshore deepwater work is highly specialised, largely done from vessels, and staffed on rotation. Onshore work looks much more like ordinary construction and drilling, and is far more accessible to Namibian businesses and workers in the near term. Onshore also brings land, community and environmental questions that offshore does not.

Upstream, midstream, downstream

The industry divides itself into three parts, and knowing which one you are talking about saves a lot of confusion.

The three streams
StreamWhat it coversNamibian relevance
UpstreamFinding and producing: exploration, appraisal, development and productionWhere everything currently is. The Petroleum Act and the new local content policy both govern upstream
MidstreamMoving and storing: pipelines, shipping, terminals and processingLargely still to come, and the area where port and logistics opportunities sit
DownstreamRefining, distribution and retail: fuel, gas and petrochemicalsAlready exists in Namibia through fuel distribution, but sits outside the upstream local content policy

When someone says the local content policy applies to them, the first question is which stream they are in. The policy is an upstream policy.

Blocks, licences and who holds what

A block is a defined area, on land or at sea, mapped by the Minister. Namibian licences are granted over blocks, which is why you see names like Block 2913B.

The Petroleum (Exploration and Production) Act 2 of 1991 provides for three licence types, and these are legal terms rather than industry slang.

Licence types under the Petroleum Act
LicenceWhat it allowsTerm
ReconnaissancePreliminary surveying, usually seismic, without exclusive rights to produce2 years, renewable
ExplorationExploring for petroleum in the block, including drilling exploration and appraisal wells4 years, renewable in further periods
ProductionDeveloping and producing petroleum from a defined production areaUp to 25 years, renewable once for up to 10

You will also hear the abbreviation PEL, which stands for petroleum exploration licence. PEL 39, PEL 83, PEL 85 and PEL 73 are the licences behind most of the names in the news.

Operator and partner

Almost no oil block is held by one company. A group of companies holds percentage interests in a joint venture, and one of them is appointed operator.

The operator runs day to day operations, lets the contracts, and is usually the entity that employs or engages the workforce. The other participants are partners or non-operating partners. They pay their share of the costs and take their share of production, but they do not run the work.

This distinction is the one that matters most commercially. If you want to supply services to a block, the operator is who you sell to. Approaching a non-operating partner will be polite and largely fruitless.

Where NAMCOR sits

The National Petroleum Corporation of Namibia holds a participating interest in the major blocks, typically around ten percent, and government has signalled an intention to increase state participation over time. NAMCOR is a partner rather than the operator on those blocks, so it is not the entity letting the day to day contracts.

FID, and why it is the date that matters

FID stands for final investment decision. It is the formal decision by the joint venture partners to commit the capital and build the project.

Before FID, spending is comparatively small, contracts are short, and everything remains reversible. After FID, construction and fabrication contracts are let, vessels and equipment are booked, and hiring and procurement begin in volume.

If you take one thing from this page, take this. A discovery is not a project. Companies announce discoveries regularly, and some of them never become anything. One international major wrote down a substantial amount on a Namibian licence in 2025 after drilling a series of wells. FID is the point at which the money becomes real.

Anchor your workforce plan and your business plan to an expected FID, not to a press release about a discovery.

Wells, and the difference between them

  • An exploration well is drilled to find out whether there is petroleum at all.
  • An appraisal well is drilled after a discovery to work out how big it is and how well it flows, so the partners can decide whether it is commercially developable. Namibia has been in an appraisal phase for several years.
  • A production well is drilled to actually produce, once the field is being developed.
  • A well test or flow test measures how much the well produces, usually quoted in barrels per day. It is one of the strongest indicators of whether a discovery is worth developing.

FPSO and subsea tie back

An FPSO is a floating production, storage and offloading vessel. It is a ship shaped facility moored above a deepwater field, which processes the oil, stores it, and offloads it into tankers. It avoids the need for a long pipeline to shore, which is why it suits fields that are far offshore and in deep water.

A subsea tie back means the wells sit on the seabed and are connected by pipework to that floating facility rather than to a fixed platform.

For employment purposes this shape matters. A development built around an FPSO creates a large amount of offshore rotational work, a large amount of marine and logistics activity through the ports, and comparatively less permanent onshore industrial employment than a refinery or a land based plant would.

Barrels, and the numbers you will see quoted

  • Barrel, abbreviated bbl. The standard unit for oil.
  • bbl/d, barrels per day. A production rate.
  • Recoverable resources. The amount thought to be producible, which is always less than what is in the ground.
  • mmboe, million barrels of oil equivalent. A way of expressing oil and gas together.
  • mmscf/d, million standard cubic feet per day. A gas production rate.

When you see a discovery described as several hundred million barrels, that is the resource. The production rate, in barrels per day, is what determines how big the operation on the ground actually is.

Two more you will hear

Local content. In Namibian usage, the added value to the Namibian economy through the use of Namibian labour, goods and services, companies, ownership and financing in the upstream sector. We unpack it in what local content actually means.

Namibianisation. Not a statutory term, but widely used to describe the progressive replacement of expatriate staff with Namibians through training and succession. The nearest thing to a legal foundation for it is the understudy requirement in the Affirmative Action Act, covered in employing non-Namibians in the sector.

Where Namibia actually is

To put the words in context, as at August 2026 the picture is roughly this. Several significant discoveries have been made offshore in the Orange Basin and are being appraised. No offshore oil project had taken a final investment decision. First oil is generally discussed as a 2029 or 2030 proposition at the earliest. A gas to power project in the south may reach a decision sooner. Onshore testing continues in the Kavango basin.

That is a sector in the appraisal and preparation phase, not a producing one. For Namibian businesses that is genuinely good news, because it means there is still time to be ready.
